extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of comparative religion, mythology, and cultural history; general educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and classification of beliefs about the afterlife across multiple cultures (Egyptian, Assyrian, Babylonian, Hebrew, Greek, Celtic, Mesoamerican, Indigenous Americas, African, Oceanic). Identifies patterns, evolutionary stages, and cultural determinants that shape concepts of heaven, hell, and the underworld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of judgment, retribution, and reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a culture's afterlife includes moral judgment and punitive or rewarding consequences for deeds in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues that among the classical religions of antiquity (Egyptian, Babylonian, Hebrew) 'the idea of judgment, retribution, and reward arose' in connection with their places of bliss and punishment. By contrast, many 'savage' or primitive societies view the afterlife as a mere extension of earthly life without moral retribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afterlife mirrors earthly life (continuity vs transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the future dwelling-place of the soul is essentially a continuation of terrestrial existence (social structures, activities, status) or a transformed/spiritualized state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that in many 'savage' societies the dead continue much as before (hunt, garden, social roles), e.g., African, American Indian, and Oceanic beliefs, whereas more advanced systems may propose transformed, immortal, or spiritual bodies (e.g., Jewish resurrection and Pauline metaphor of seed/sown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Access rules tied to social role or manner of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific eligibility rules determining who attains particular afterlife realms (e.g., warriors, those killed by water, sacrificial victims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the Teutonic and Mexican warrior-paradises (Valhalla; the sun for warriors slain in battle), Tlalocan for those who died through water-related causes (lepers, victims of lightning), and Aztec cosmology where different deaths lead to different heavens. The page emphasizes that 'a place of bliss is reserved, in most cases, for the warrior' in barbaric stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of civilization/ethical development with afterlife complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which ethical notions (sin, repentance, judgment) and complex afterlife geography develop with social/civilizational advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author presents an evolutionary framework: primitive = mere home of the dead; barbaric = emergence of rulers/arch-devils and warrior paradises; higher civilization = ethical significance culminating in judgment and reward/punishment. 'Only in the higher reaches of civilization does any idea of judgment, retribution, or reward ... enter into the future life.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification of celestial bodies and astral theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which gods/afterlife realms are identified with stars, planets, and heavenly bodies, shaping conceptions of heaven and divine residence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Babylonian astral system is given as an example: 'The idea of personifying the stars and planets ... had the outstanding feature that occurrences on earth closely corresponded to the movements in Heaven.' Such identification made it 'easy ... to conceive gods as dwelling in the sky.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural/corn-spirit influence on lords of the dead
rubrics_metrics.description: Role of agricultural cults and corn-spirit motifs in shaping the character and functions of underworld deities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that many underworld rulers (e.g., Persephone, Osiris, daughters of Xibalba) derive from or were grafted onto agricultural/corn-spirit myths, explaining attributes and seasonal motifs of the underworld: 'The myth of Persephone well illustrates the adaptation of a corn-spirit to the lordship (or ladyship) of Hades.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography of afterlife (sky/west vs subterranean)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural reasoning for placing paradise in the sky/west and regions of woe underground or remote; symbolic associations driving geographic placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains why many peoples locate Heaven in the west or sky (sunset association, the sun as source of good) and place realms of woe in an underworld. Example: 'many various peoples... believed their Paradise... to be in the west, where sinks the dying sun.' In contrast, astral-theologized cultures place gods in the sky because of star-personification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional cultural patterns (e.g., Greece)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that particular cultures may deviate from the general evolutionary pattern and require separate analytic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author highlights Greece as 'one strange exception' where ethic/philosophic influences produced different outcomes (e.g., Hades as initially a realm for all the dead, and later abstract regions Hades/Tartarus/Elysium), suggesting that philosophical rather than purely religious ethics altered Greek conceptions.
